p.src: Now Sun Quan sought counsel from Lü Meng. Lü Meng said, “I judge that Guan’s forces are few, so he will surely not flee by the main road. Directly north of Maicheng lies a steep and narrow path; he is certain to take that route. Order Zhu Ran to lead five thousand picked troops and lie in ambush twenty li north of Maicheng. When his army arrives, they must not engage it directly, but only follow and strike from behind. His men will certainly have no heart for battle and will flee toward Linju. Then have Pan Zhang lead five hundred picked troops and lie in ambush on a secluded mountain path at Linju; Guan will thus be captured. Now send the officers and men to attack every gate, leaving only the north gate open and waiting for him to flee through it.” On hearing the plan, Sun Quan ordered Lü Fan to divine the outcome once more. When the hexagram was cast, Lü Fan reported, “This sign foretells that the enemy will flee northwest. Tonight, at the hour of the Boar, he will surely be taken.” Sun Quan was overjoyed and ordered Zhu Ran and Pan Zhang to lead their two picked forces away and set their ambushes according to his commands.

p.src: Meanwhile, Lord Guan counted the cavalry and infantry in Maicheng and found that only a little over three hundred remained; their provisions and fodder were exhausted as well. That night, the Wu troops outside the walls called out the names of men in each unit, and many climbed over the walls and deserted. Nor was there any sign of the relief force. At a loss for a plan, he said to Wang Fu, “I regret that I did not heed your words before! Now that the danger is upon us, what are we to do?” Wang Fu wept as he replied, “As matters stand today, even if Ziya returned to life, he could devise no remedy.” Zhao Lei said, “The relief troops from Shangyong have not come because Liu Feng and Meng Da are holding their forces back. Why not abandon this isolated city, flee into Xichuan, reorganize the army, and then return to recover what has been lost?” Lord Guan said, “That is what I intend as well.” He then climbed the wall to survey the ground. Seeing that there were few enemy troops outside the north gate, he asked a local inhabitant, “What is the terrain like northward from here?” The man replied, “From here onward there are only secluded mountain paths, but they lead through to Xichuan.” Lord Guan said, “Tonight we shall take that route.” Wang Fu remonstrated, “There may be an ambush on the narrow path. You should take the main road.” Lord Guan said, “Even if there is an ambush, what have I to fear?” He immediately gave orders for the mounted and foot soldiers to put their equipment in order and prepare to leave the city. Wang Fu wept and said, “My lord, take every care upon the road! I shall remain with over a hundred men and defend this city to the death; even if the city falls, I shall never surrender! I ask only that my lord return swiftly to our aid!”

p.src: Lord Guan also wept as he took his leave. He left Zhou Cang to defend Maicheng together with Wang Fu. Lord Guan himself, with Guan Ping and Zhao Lei, led the remaining two hundred-odd men in a sudden dash through the north gate. Lord Guan advanced with his blade held crosswise. After the first watch, when they had gone some twenty li, gongs and drums suddenly sounded together in a mountain hollow and tremendous battle cries arose as a force appeared. At its head was the general Zhu Ran, who spurred forward with leveled spear and cried, “Yun-chang, flee no farther! Surrender while there is still time and spare yourself death!” Enraged, Lord Guan urged on his horse, whirled his blade, and engaged him. Zhu Ran turned and fled, and Lord Guan pursued and struck after him. At a roll of the drum, ambushers rose on every side. Lord Guan dared not remain in battle and fled toward the narrow road to Linju. Zhu Ran led his troops in a pursuing attack. The soldiers following Lord Guan gradually dwindled in number. Before they had gone four or five li, battle cries again thundered ahead and a great blaze of torches arose as Pan Zhang galloped toward them, brandishing his blade. Lord Guan, furious, swung his blade to meet him; after only three bouts, Pan Zhang fled in defeat. Lord Guan dared not linger in combat and hurried away along the mountain path. Guan Ping came up from behind and reported that Zhao Lei had been killed amid the mêlée. Overcome with grief and alarm, Lord Guan ordered Guan Ping to guard the rear while he himself opened the way ahead; scarcely more than ten men now followed them. They reached Jueshi, where mountains rose on both sides and the slopes were overgrown with reeds, withered grass, and tangled trees. The fifth watch was now nearly over. As they pressed on, a shout arose and ambushers poured out from both sides, raising long hooks and lassos together; first they tripped the horse beneath Lord Guan. Lord Guan tumbled from his horse and was captured by Ma Zhong, a subordinate general of Pan Zhang. Learning that his father had been taken, Guan Ping rushed to the rescue; but Pan Zhang and Zhu Ran led their troops up from behind and surrounded him on every side. Guan Ping fought alone until his strength was spent, and he too was captured. At daybreak, Sun Quan heard that Lord Guan and his son had been captured. Overjoyed, he assembled his generals in his command tent.

p.src: Before long, Ma Zhong brought Lord Guan forward under heavy guard. Sun Quan said, “I have long admired your illustrious virtue, General, and wished to bind our houses in marriage. Why did you reject me? You always considered yourself invincible under Heaven; how is it that today you have been captured by me? Will you now submit to Sun Quan?” Lord Guan cursed him in a stern voice: “Blue-eyed brat! Purple-bearded rat! I swore brotherhood with Imperial Uncle Liu in the Peach Garden and vowed to uphold the House of Han. How could I associate with a traitor to Han such as you? Today I have mistakenly fallen into a treacherous scheme; death is all that remains. Why waste further words?” Sun Quan turned to his officers and said, “Yun-chang is a hero of the age, and I cherish him deeply. I wish to treat him with honor and persuade him to surrender. What say you?” Zuo Xian, the Registrar, said, “You must not. When Cao Cao once had this man, he enfeoffed and ennobled him, holding a small banquet every three days and a great banquet every five; when he mounted, he was presented with gold, and when he dismounted, with silver. Yet despite such favor and courtesy, Cao Cao could not keep him: he let him pass the barriers, slay the generals, and depart. Thus today Cao Cao has instead been driven so hard by him that he nearly wished to move the capital to escape his edge. Now that my lord has captured him, unless he is removed at once, I fear he will leave future trouble.” Sun Quan pondered for a long while, then said, “These words are right.” He then ordered the prisoners taken out. Thus Lord Guan and his son were both put to death. It was the twelfth month of winter in the twenty-fourth year of Jian’an. Lord Guan was fifty-eight years old at his death. p.src: But Lord Guan’s heroic spirit did not disperse. Drifting on and on, it came at last to a mountain in Dangyang County of Jingmen Prefecture, named Mount Yuquan. On the mountain lived an aged monk whose Dharma name was Pujing. He had formerly been the abbot of Zhenguo Temple at Sishui Pass; later, while wandering throughout the realm, he came to this place. Finding its mountains fair and waters lovely, he built a thatched hermitage there and spent each day in meditation and contemplation of the Way; he had with him only a young acolyte, who begged food for their sustenance. That night the moon was bright and the wind clear. After the third watch, while Pujing sat silently in his hermitage, he suddenly heard someone in the air cry loudly, “Give me back my head!” Pujing raised his face and looked intently. In the air he saw a man riding the Red Hare and carrying the Green Dragon blade; on his left followed a fair-faced general, and on his right a black-faced man with a bristling beard; together they lowered their cloud and descended upon the summit of Mount Yuquan. Pujing recognized Lord Guan. Striking his door with the fly whisk in his hand, he called, “Where is Yun-chang?”

I beg your pure instruction to guide me from my delusion.” Pujing said, “What was wrong before and seems right now need no longer be discussed. Later consequences and former causes fail neither party by the slightest degree. p.src: Now Sun Quan, having slain Guan Gong, took possession of all Jing and Xiang, rewarded the three armies, and held a great banquet for his commanders to celebrate their victory; he seated Lü Meng in the place of honor and said to the assembled generals, “For long I could not obtain Jingzhou, yet now it has fallen into my hands with scarcely an effort. This is all Ziming's achievement.” Lü Meng repeatedly declined the praise and offered his thanks. Sun Quan said, “In former days Zhou Lang possessed extraordinary heroic strategy and defeated Cao Cao at Red Cliffs, but unhappily died young, whereupon Lu Zijing succeeded him. When Zijing first met me, he immediately spoke of the grand strategy for an imperial enterprise. That was his first admirable merit; when Cao Cao marched east, everyone urged me to surrender, but Zijing alone advised me to summon Gongjin and meet Cao Cao in battle. That was his second admirable merit. His one failing was that he advised me to lend Jingzhou to Liu Bei. But now Ziming has devised and settled a plan that seized Jingzhou at once. In this he far surpasses Zijing and Zhou Lang.” He then personally poured wine and bestowed it on Lü Meng. Lü Meng took the wine and was about to drink when suddenly he hurled the cup to the ground, seized Sun Quan with one hand, and fiercely cursed him: “Green-eyed brat! Purple-bearded rat, do you still know who I am?” The generals were greatly alarmed. When they rushed to intervene, Lü Meng shoved Sun Quan down, strode forward, and sat in Sun Quan's place. His brows stood on end and his eyes opened wide as he roared, “For more than thirty years since I first defeated the Yellow Turbans, I have ranged unconquered across the realm. Now you have brought me down in a single day by treacherous design. In life I could not devour your flesh, but in death I shall pursue the soul of that villain Lü! I am Guan Yunchang, Marquis of Hanshou Village!” Sun Quan was terrified and hastily led all his officers and soldiers, high and low, in bowing before him. Then they saw Lü Meng collapse to the ground, bleeding from all seven apertures, and die. None of the generals who witnessed it was free from fear. Sun Quan had Lü Meng's body placed in a coffin and buried, and posthumously granted him the titles Administrator of Nanjun and Marquis of Chanling; he ordered Lü Meng's son Lü Ba to inherit the marquisate. From that time onward, Sun Quan remained endlessly astonished by the affair of Guan Gong.

p.src: Suddenly it was reported that Zhang Zhao had arrived from Jianye. Sun Quan summoned him and questioned him. Zhang Zhao said, “My lord, now that you have destroyed Guan Gong and his son, disaster for Jiangdong cannot be far away. When Guan Gong swore brotherhood with Liu Bei in the Peach Garden, they vowed to share life and death. Liu Bei now commands the armies of the Two Riverlands; in addition, he has Zhuge Liang's strategy and the valor of Zhang, Huang, Ma, and Zhao. If Liu Bei learns that Yunchang and his son have been slain, he will surely mobilize the entire strength of his state and fight with all his might to avenge them. I fear Eastern Wu will find it difficult to withstand him.” Sun Quan was horrified on hearing this. Stamping his foot, he said, “I have miscalculated! What can be done now?” Zhang Zhao said, “Do not worry, my lord. I have a plan that will keep the armies of Western Shu from invading Eastern Wu and make Jingzhou secure as solid rock.” Sun Quan asked what the plan was. Zhang Zhao said, “Cao Cao now commands a million men and watches all the realm like a tiger. Eager to avenge himself, Liu Bei will surely seek an alliance with Cao Cao. If armies from both quarters join forces and advance, Eastern Wu will be in danger. We should first send Guan Gong's head on to Cao Cao, making Liu Bei plainly believe that Cao Cao instigated the deed. He will then bitterly hate Cao Cao. The armies of Western Shu will march not against Wu, but against Wei. We can watch which side wins and use the opportunity to accomplish our own ends. This is the best policy.”

p.src: Sun Quan followed his advice and at once dispatched an envoy, who placed Guan Gong's head in a wooden casket and carried it through the night with all speed to Cao Cao. At the time, Cao Cao was returning to Luoyang with his army from Mopo. Hearing that Eastern Wu had sent Guan Gong's head, he rejoiced and said, “Now that Yunchang is dead, I can sleep soundly at night.” One man below the steps came forward and said, “This is Eastern Wu's scheme to shift disaster onto us.” Cao Cao looked and saw that it was his Registrar, Sima Yi. Cao Cao asked his reason, and Sima Yi replied, “Long ago, when Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei swore brotherhood in the Peach Garden, they vowed to share life and death. Now Eastern Wu has slain Guan Gong and fears Liu Bei's vengeance. Therefore they have presented his head to Your Majesty so that Liu Bei will transfer his anger to you and attack Wei rather than Wu, while they exploit the opportunity to pursue their own designs.” Cao Cao said, “Zhongda speaks truly. By what plan can I escape this?” Sima Yi said, “This matter is very easily handled. Your Majesty should carve a body from fragrant wood to accompany Guan Gong's head and bury him with the rites accorded a great minister. When Liu Bei learns of it, he will surely hate Sun Quan deeply and exert all his strength in a southern campaign. We shall then watch which side wins: if Shu prevails, we attack Wu; if Wu prevails, we attack Shu. Once we obtain either one of the two, the other will not endure for long.” Cao Cao was delighted and followed his plan, then summoned the envoy from Wu. The wooden casket was presented. Cao Cao opened the casket and looked inside; Guan Gong's face appeared just as it had in life. Cao Cao laughed and said, “Lord Yunchang, have you been well since last we parted?” Before he finished speaking, Guan Gong's mouth opened, his eyes moved, and his beard and hair bristled. Cao Cao collapsed in fright. The officials hurried to revive him. Only after a long while did he regain consciousness, and he turned to them and said, “General Guan is truly a god of heaven!” The envoy from Wu also told Cao Cao how Guan Gong had manifested his divine power, possessed Lü Meng, cursed Sun Quan, and pursued Lü Meng to his death. Cao Cao grew still more afraid. He arranged sacrificial animals and wine as offerings, had a body carved from agarwood, and buried Guan Gong outside Luoyang's southern gate with the rites accorded a prince and marquis. He ordered all officials, high and low, to attend the funeral, personally performed the rites, posthumously entitled Guan Gong Prince of Jing, and appointed an officer to guard the tomb; he then sent the envoy from Wu back to Jiangdong.

u.src: Sun Quan followed his advice and at once dispatched an envoy, who placed Guan Gong's head in a wooden casket and carried it through the night with all speed to Cao Cao.

At the time, Cao Cao was returning to Luoyang with his army from Mopo. Hearing that Eastern Wu had sent Guan Gong's head, he rejoiced and said, “Now that Yunchang is dead, I can sleep soundly at night.”
One man below the steps came forward and said, “This is Eastern Wu's scheme to shift disaster onto us.”
Cao Cao looked and saw that it was his Registrar, Sima Yi.
Cao Cao asked his reason, and Sima Yi replied, “Long ago, when Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei swore brotherhood in the Peach Garden, they vowed to share life and death.

Now Eastern Wu has slain Guan Gong and fears Liu Bei's vengeance. Therefore they have presented his head to Your Majesty so that Liu Bei will transfer his anger to you and attack Wei rather than Wu, while they exploit the opportunity to pursue their own designs.”
Cao Cao said, “Zhongda speaks truly.
By what plan can I escape this?”
Sima Yi said, “This matter is very easily handled.
Your Majesty should carve a body from fragrant wood to accompany Guan Gong's head and bury him with the rites accorded a great minister.
When Liu Bei learns of it, he will surely hate Sun Quan deeply and exert all his strength in a southern campaign.
We shall then watch which side wins: if Shu prevails, we attack Wu; if Wu prevails, we attack Shu.
Once we obtain either one of the two, the other will not endure for long.”
Cao Cao was delighted and followed his plan, then summoned the envoy from Wu.
The wooden casket was presented.
Cao Cao opened the casket and looked inside; Guan Gong's face appeared just as it had in life.
Cao Cao laughed and said, “Lord Yunchang, have you been well since last we parted?”
Before he finished speaking, Guan Gong's mouth opened, his eyes moved, and his beard and hair bristled. Cao Cao collapsed in fright.
The officials hurried to revive him. Only after a long while did he regain consciousness, and he turned to them and said, “General Guan is truly a god of heaven!”
The envoy from Wu also told Cao Cao how Guan Gong had manifested his divine power, possessed Lü Meng, cursed Sun Quan, and pursued Lü Meng to his death.

Cao Cao grew still more afraid. He arranged sacrificial animals and wine as offerings, had a body carved from agarwood, and buried Guan Gong outside Luoyang's southern gate with the rites accorded a prince and marquis.
He ordered all officials, high and low, to attend the funeral, personally performed the rites, posthumously entitled Guan Gong Prince of Jing, and appointed an officer to guard the tomb;
he then sent the envoy from Wu back to Jiangdong.

p.src: Now the King of Hanzhong returned from Dongchuan to Chengdu, and Fa Zheng memorialized, “My lord, your former wife has passed away; Lady Sun has also returned south and may never come back. The proper relations of human society must not be neglected. You must take a royal consort to assist in the governance of your household.” The King of Hanzhong accepted his advice. Fa Zheng further memorialized, “Wu Yi has a younger sister who is both beautiful and virtuous. I have heard that a physiognomist once read her features and foretold that she would attain the highest nobility. She was formerly betrothed to Liu Mao, a son of Liu Yan; but Liu Mao died young. She has remained a widow to this day. Your Majesty could take her as your consort.” The King of Hanzhong said, “Liu Mao and I belong to the same clan; propriety forbids it.” Fa Zheng said, “In closeness of kin, how is this different from Duke Wen of Jin and Huai Ying?” The King of Hanzhong thereupon consented and took Lady Wu as his royal consort. She later bore two sons: the elder was Liu Yong, courtesy name Gongshou; the younger was Liu Li, courtesy name Fengxiao.

p.src: Now in the eastern and western Riverlands the people lived in peace, the state prospered, and the crops yielded an abundant harvest. Suddenly a man arrived from Jingzhou and reported that Eastern Wu had sought a marriage alliance with Guan Gong, but Guan Gong had firmly rejected it. Kongming said, “Jingzhou is in danger! Someone must be sent to relieve Guan Gong and bring him back.” While they were discussing the matter, messengers bearing victory reports from Jingzhou arrived one after another. Before many days had passed, Guan Xing arrived and gave a full account of the flooding of the Seven Armies. Suddenly another mounted courier came and reported that Guan Gong had erected many beacon posts along the riverbank and arranged such rigorous defenses that nothing could possibly go wrong. At this, Xuande's mind was set at ease.

At this, Xuande's mind was set at ease.

p.src: Suddenly, one day, Xuande felt his whole body tremble, and could find no ease whether walking or sitting; when night came, he could not sleep peacefully, so he rose and sat in his private chamber, reading by candlelight. Growing dazed and confused, he laid his head upon the desk and fell asleep; suddenly a chill wind swept through the room, and the lamp went out, then flared alight again. Raising his head, he saw a man standing beneath it. Xuande asked, “Who are you, to enter my private chamber at this dead hour of night?” The man did not answer. Bewildered and suspicious, Xuande rose to look more closely. It was Lord Guan, moving to and fro in the lamplight and trying to avoid him. Xuande said, “Worthy brother, I trust you have been well since we parted! For you to come here so late at night, some grave event must have occurred. The bond between us is that of flesh and blood; why do you avoid me?” Lord Guan wept and said, “I beg you, elder brother, to raise an army and avenge my wrong!” As soon as he had spoken, a chill wind sprang up violently, and Lord Guan vanished. Xuande awoke with a start and realized it had been a dream. It was then precisely the third watch. Deeply troubled, Xuande hurried to the front hall and sent someone to summon Kongming. Kongming entered and presented himself. Xuande related every detail of the ominous dream. Kongming said, “This dream came only because Your Majesty has Lord Guan constantly in mind. Why entertain such grave doubts?” Xuande remained beset by doubts, but Kongming repeatedly soothed him with reassuring words.

p.src: Kongming took his leave, and outside the middle gate he encountered Xu Jing coming toward him. Xu Jing said, “I had just gone to the military adviser’s residence to report a secret matter. Hearing that you had entered the palace, I came here expressly to find you.” Kongming asked, “What secret matter is this?” Xu Jing replied, “I have just heard people outside saying that Lü Meng of Eastern Wu has already seized Jingzhou by surprise and that Lord Guan has been slain. I therefore came especially to report it to you in secret.” Kongming said, “When I observed the heavens at night, I saw a general’s star fall over the region of Jing and Chu. I knew then that Yunchang must have met with disaster, but I feared the king would be overcome with grief and therefore dared not speak of it.” While the two were speaking, a man suddenly emerged from within the hall, seized Kongming by the sleeve, and cried, “Why did you conceal such dreadful news from me?” Kongming looked and saw that it was Xuande. Kongming and Xu Jing reported, “What we were just discussing is all mere hearsay and cannot yet be fully believed. We beg Your Majesty to set your mind at ease and not give way to anxiety.” Xuande said, “Yunchang and I swore to live and die together; if harm has befallen him, how can I go on living alone?”

p.src: While Kongming and Xu Jing were trying to console him, an attendant suddenly reported, “Ma Liang and Yi Ji have arrived.” Xuande hastily summoned them and questioned them. The two gave a full account of the loss of Jingzhou and of Lord Guan’s defeat and plea for aid, then presented his memorial. Before it could be opened and read, a court attendant reported that Liao Hua had arrived from Jingzhou. Xuande hastily summoned him inside. Liao Hua fell to the ground, weeping and bowing, and reported in detail how Liu Feng and Meng Da had refused to send reinforcements. Xuande was aghast and cried, “If that is so, my brother is lost!” Kongming said, “For Liu Feng and Meng Da to behave with such insolence is a crime for which even death cannot atone! Let Your Majesty set your mind at ease. I, Liang, shall personally lead a force to relieve the urgent peril in Jingzhou.” Xuande wept and said, “If harm has befallen Yunchang, I will never continue living alone! Tomorrow I shall personally lead an army to rescue Yunchang!” He at once dispatched a messenger to Langzhong to inform Yide, while sending others to muster the troops. Before daybreak, several reports arrived in succession, saying that Lord Guan had fled by night toward Linju, only to be captured by the generals of Wu; refusing in righteous loyalty to submit, father and son had returned to the spirits. When Xuande heard this, he gave one great cry and fell senseless to the ground. Indeed:
